claims.text: The initial material is equiatomic NbMoTaW with a single-phase BCC microstructure.
Forging at approximately 1000–1200 °C followed by short annealing will refine the grain and subgrain structures of NbMoTaW.
The treatment will stabilize a hierarchical BCC grain structure containing dense subgrain boundaries.
The treatment will increase the room-temperature ductility of NbMoTaW.
The treatment will improve the irradiation tolerance of NbMoTaW.
The treatment will preserve the high-temperature mechanical strength of NbMoTaW.
The treatment will preserve the single-phase BCC stability of NbMoTaW.
Refined grain and subgrain boundaries will act as effective sinks for dislocations, helium bubbles, dislocation loops, and other irradiation-induced defects.
Moderate-temperature forging introduces high-angle grain boundaries in NbMoTaW.
The introduced boundaries enhance dislocation mobility and defect annihilation.
Enhanced dislocation mobility increases room-temperature ductility.
Defect annihilation at the introduced boundaries reduces radiation-induced defect accumulation.
Short annealing at 1000–1200 °C prevents unwanted precipitation.
Preventing precipitation preserves the single-phase BCC matrix and its high-temperature strength.
The treated alloy will exhibit a 50–100% increase in room-temperature ductility relative to as-cast NbMoTaW.
The treated alloy will maintain excellent strength up to approximately 1600 °C.
Following helium irradiation at approximately 800–1000 °C, the treated alloy will have lower helium-bubble density and less irradiation damage than as-cast NbMoTaW.
Keeping forging and annealing within 1000–1200 °C avoids excessive grain growth and second-phase precipitation.
Temperatures or irradiation doses beyond normal reactor conditions may impair the beneficial subgrain structure.
It is unverified whether subgrain boundaries alone can prevent irradiation-induced amorphization or precipitation in NbMoTaW.
